pages.title: Nbody: retain state across all timesteps

blocks.text: The newest complete session reproduces the exact flat_pow improvement: median runtime falls from 227.19575 to 143.3736875 ms per 20,000-step unit, a 36.89% reduction (1.5846x). The previous full run showed 37.53% with the same source. This is confirmation under another collection block, not a new nbody optimization; grouped remains the earlier 3.40% intermediate.

rows: Explain contributions; no extra speedup claimed.

blocks.text: The reference is the pyperformance five-body gravitational benchmark: Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Each step processes ten unordered pairs, updates both bodies' velocities, then advances five positions. A unit has 20,000 steps at dt = 0.01: 200,000 pair updates and 100,000 position updates. Sixteen timed units accumulate state through 320,000 steps; they do not restart from the initial orbit.

BODIES maps names to tuples containing mutable position and velocity lists plus mass. SYSTEM and PAIRS alias those lists. Python floats are boxed objects. Dependencies are pyperf and standard Python; the final optimized software uses no external numeric library. All inputs and masses are read from supplied state; no trajectories or answers are precomputed.

Conceptually, for each pair delta = r1 - r2 and mag = dt * (delta dot delta) ** (-1.5). The two velocity increments are opposite, weighted by the other body's mass. Only after all ten pairs does each position advance by dt * velocity. Energy reporting sums kinetic energy and negative pair potential; momentum offset initializes the reference body before timing. The implementation preserves the reference's exact expression order, not just these real-number identities.

The wrapper loads fresh upstream state for each independent measurement and calls upstream.bench_nbody. Momentum offset occurs before its internal timer. Each timed unit runs energy reporting, advance, then energy reporting. The optimized wrapper substitutes only advance; validation, loading and writeback in that function remain timed. Energy reporting and the upstream loop remain unchanged.

Newest matched pair: results/nbody_baseline_20260920-080806_16940 and results/nbody_optimized_20260920-081744_16940. Comparison: results/session_all_20260920-074308_674/comparison_nbody. Kernel flat_pow and all captured source hashes match current files.

pages.title: Use independent instruments for different questions

blocks.text: The target is Ubuntu 22.04.5, Linux 5.15.0-1106-kvm, one virtual CPU exposing an Intel Xeon E5-2630 v3 at 2.40 GHz. Clean timing uses release CPython 3.10.12, CPU 0 affinity, a fixed hash seed and cyclic GC disabled. The VM governor is unavailable; host scheduling, frequency and contention are not fully controlled. These are measurements of this guest, not bare-metal Haswell limits.

blocks.text: The custom wrapper calls the actual upstream bench function and uses its timer. A minimal pyperf import stub exposes time.perf_counter; it does not implement pyperf.Runner. Thus this is an upstream-workload experiment through a custom harness, alongside a separate official pyperformance baseline run. That distinction does not invalidate the experiment; the workload, timer boundaries and comparison controls must be explicit.

Runtime reduction = 100 x (1 - optimized median / baseline median). Speedup = baseline median / optimized median. We use runtime reduction for the declared 7% target. CV = sample standard deviation / mean. Samples from separate TXT and CSV perf invocations are not pooled.

pages.title: Container overhead was real, but not the whole cost

blocks.text: A flame graph is an aggregation of sampled call stacks, not a timeline. Width is inclusive sampled weight; height is stack depth, not elapsed time. Self weight counts only samples whose leaf is that symbol. Children weight includes descendants and overlaps other ancestors. The libc start routine can therefore have a huge inclusive share while doing little direct work. Aggregate a function across every folded stack: the top-30 listing is incomplete, and repeated appearances must not be mistaken for separate causes.

In the newest baseline native profile, PyObject_GetItem and PyObject_SetItem subtrees cover 206 of 1,175 samples (17.53%). Evaluator self weight is 526 (44.77%). Float operators, binary dispatch, boxing and release are also prominent. These categories overlap when inclusive; do not sum them into a partition of runtime.

The source explains the stack evidence. Every pair unpacks positions and masses; each v[i] update reads and writes a list element through Python's generic numeric/container machinery. A cache hit still needs interpreter instructions, bounds/index handling, reference updates and dispatch. Keeping a float reference in a local avoids those container operations even when the entire physical working set fits in cache.

rows: 30 initial reads + 30 final writes per advance, outside the timestep loop

blocks.text: These are source-operation counts, not machine-load counts or runtime percentages. Entry shape validation and mass/container access are excluded from the component count. All float arithmetic remains: 5.4 million float-result expressions per unit. Locals still hold boxed floats, and interpreter freelists can reuse storage; neither an expression count nor a constructor call equals a fresh malloc.

CPython is a bytecode interpreter, not an AST interpreter. _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault includes bytecode execution, operand handling, loop control and reference work; its self share is not pure call overhead. Debug checks and different code generation change costs. High IPC and few cache misses support an instruction-work hypothesis but do not identify a precise hardware stall limit. Reject negative top-down fractions and unsupported PMU events rather than interpreting them as valid measurements or zeros.

pages.title: Why grouped was modest; why flattening is different

blocks.text: grouped retains the first body's position and velocity across its consecutive partners, writes its velocity once per group, and updates the second body immediately. It preserves upstream pair and arithmetic order, including pow. It removes 24% of logical component accesses but still traverses groups, unpacks tuples and reloads state on every timestep. Four partner iterators per step add overhead. Retaining pow was intentional, not an experiment defect.

flat_pow loads all 30 position/velocity components into scalar locals once per advance, retains them through all timesteps, explicitly expands the ten pairs and five position updates in their original order, and writes state back once. It simultaneously removes most state subscripting, repeated unpacking and short-loop traversal. The outer timestep loop, actual physics, power expression and update ordering remain.

The specialization supports five bodies, canonical ordered pairs, distinct ordinary position/velocity lists of floats, float dt and nonnegative integer steps. Validation rejects unsupported shapes. It preserves list identity and successful-call state; delayed writeback does not preserve partial updates on exceptions, signal-time observations or arbitrary aliased/custom containers. This is an explicit benchmark contract, not universal Python API equivalence.

blocks.text: A repeated small saving matters over 20,000 steps, but repetition multiplies both old and new work; it does not automatically multiply percentage speedup. The grouped and flat results show that the scope of state reuse, not merely the presence of local variables, determines the impact.

Acceptance for grouped and flat_pow requires finite, bit-identical energy and all 30 state components, checked as binary floating-point values. Energy alone is insufficient: different trajectories can share a similar total energy. Tests cover zero steps, small trajectories, randomized valid states/masses, list identity, invalid layout rejection and full accumulated batches.

The saved optimized gate in this new session compares the complete reference and candidate 16 x 20,000-step batch: energy -0.1690801979358367 and every state bit match for grouped and flat_pow. Earlier full results saved only a one-unit automatic gate; the new artifact closes that batch-evidence gap. The standalone baseline verifier still checks one unit despite a loops=16 phase label; the independent reference run inside the optimized gate provides the full comparison. The existing integrated software suite passed 63 tests; no benchmark code changed in this review.

pages.title: Newest full run confirms the previous improvement

blocks.caption: Eleven fresh processes per arm; 16 accumulated units per process. Every observation retained; arms collected in separate blocks.

blocks.text: Median runtime reduction is 36.8942% (1.5846x), saving 83.8221 ms per unit. Even the slowest optimized observation beats the fastest baseline by 35.36%. This exceeds the 7% runtime criterion with wide margin; within-block dispersion is not a bound on systematic VM drift.

The preceding full run was 228.24925 -> 142.578375 ms (37.53%). Relative to that run, this baseline is 0.46% faster and flat_pow is 0.56% slower. The source is identical; the 0.64 percentage-point change is a repeat-measurement difference, not evidence of an added optimization or a code regression. Grouped remains 3.40%; the optional flat_sqrt result remains a separate approximate experiment.
Latest official pyperformance baseline: 60 values, median 228.636 ms, mean 229.411 +/- 3.439 ms. It corroborates workload scale; no optimized official-harness result exists.

pages.title: The removed work is reproduced in the new profiles

blocks.caption: Equal native work: five units per arm, debug CPython, fixed 5-million-cycle period. Item access and float lifetime rows are inclusive unions; evaluator and libm pow are self. Do not sum rows.

blocks.text: Generic item-access union falls 206 -> 2 samples and evaluator self falls 526 -> 285. Total samples fall 1,175 -> 725. The preceding run showed the same structural change (226 -> 2 item-access samples). Independent CSV counting corroborates instructions -34.82%, cycles -37.03% and L1 loads -34.50%.

Float creation inclusive samples are 71 -> 73, release 41 -> 42, and libm pow self 20 -> 19. These noisy counts support arithmetic and boxed-value lifetime work remaining. Locals have not eliminated float-result objects or the power calculation. The gain comes mainly from reducing repeated state access, unpacking and interpreter traversal.

pages.title: Read the similar stacks without missing the change

blocks.caption: Newest original native SVG overviews. Each fills its own panel despite 1,175 versus 725 total samples. Adjacent original SVGs allow zooming.

blocks.text: Both runs still enter the same upstream timed loop, call advance and execute floating-point operations through CPython. Those common stack bases dominate the visual silhouette. The flat wrapper adds a different call path, so depth is not a direct work measure. Look for the missing subscription branches and compare equal-work leaf/subtree counts instead of only the outline.

Each cProfile arm still calls the numerical advance function once per unit. Whole-process call counts include optimized-wrapper startup and validation; they do not count arithmetic bytecodes as Python calls. Most remaining work is within the long advance call. Folded aggregation of all stacks is more reliable than comparing two partial top-30 listings.

TXT and CSV counter batches agree on major instruction, cycle and load reductions. L1 misses disagree in direction between batches; generic cache events are noisy. No cache-miss improvement is established. Negative top-down fractions invalidate that decomposition and unsupported LLC events remain unavailable. These limitations do not invalidate the independent clean runtime result.

Session manifests capture the actual variant, upstream, wrapper, common/pipeline and configuration hashes; all match current files. Git metadata is disabled rather than guessed. The full saved optimized correctness gate covers reference and candidate at 16 units. However, there is no persisted phase-0 package authenticity transcript, and the embedded UNVERIFIED placeholder remains. Some phase rows stay requested despite present completed artifacts; py-spy is explicitly disabled.

The remaining bottleneck is a set of costs: arithmetic dispatch, boxed values, evaluator work and pow. An exact next software improvement must be tested against flat_pow. The new structural controls can distinguish locality from unrolling; the current aggregate speedup cannot uniquely allocate savings among them.
One ray-sphere accelerator is implemented for the project. It is relevant to raytrace; a separate exact nbody engine is deferred.

hardware/rtl/ray_sphere_accel.sv contains the sequential controller, operand/result registers, status and ready/valid protocol. The datapath uses actual unmodified BSD-licensed Berkeley HardFloat Release 1 RTL: one shared add/sub unit, one multiplier and an iterative square-root unit. There are no real-number or software-math placeholders in the synthesizable datapath.

cp = center - origin
v = (cp.x*dx + cp.y*dy) + cp.z*dz
q = (cp.x*cp.x + cp.y*cp.y) + cp.z*cp.z
disc = r*r - (q - v*v)
result = no_root if disc < 0 else v - sqrt(disc)

Each operation rounds separately to binary64, nearest-even, including gradual underflow. There is no FMA, reassociation, FP32 or approximate reciprocal root. A tangent and a negative returned distance preserve upstream behavior; software applies its original hit-selection rule. Finite inputs/intermediates, nonnegative radius and caller-normalized direction define the supported domain. Invalid/nonfinite cases return an error for CPU fallback.

HardFloat source and license: hardware/vendor/ provenance and license files. Primary specification: https://www.jhauser.us/arithmetic/HardFloat-1/doc/HardFloat-Verilog.html. Detailed ports, schedule and host format: docs/HARDWARE_DESIGN.md and hardware/.

Design reassessment: sphere intersections remain frequent, but square root is reached only 6,934 times (3.864% of 179,457 queries). The current core is a single-query sequential function with no resident scene or internal batch controller. A batched geometric core or a small reusable FP64 command engine are alternatives, not implemented replacements. More general hardware is not automatically faster; operand residency and the software offload boundary need justification.

Shared arithmetic reduces replication but constrains throughput; pipelining or multiple lanes costs area, registers and potential switching. No area/watt/achieved-clock numbers are claimed. Nbody offload still needs exact host-power semantics or an explicit different contract; this ray-sphere core does not accelerate nbody.

pages.title: New workload evidence changes the estimate

rows: 640 operand bits + 32-bit tag; distance/status/flags response; one outstanding query; ready/valid and held response.
Separate FP64 rounding, ordered expressions, caller-normalized rays; finite supported domain with CPU fallback on error.
Arithmetic/control RTL and host packing exist. Renderer batching, transport/DMA and driver remain proposed.
50 MHz target assumption; 20 cycles/miss, 80/root budget. No achieved timing or HDL simulation.

blocks.text: The full-profile math.sqrt caller map records 6,934 sphere calls; 37,715 other square roots belong to magnitude and one to import setup. Thus h = 6,934 / 179,457 = 0.0386388. Source control flow confirms that sphere calls sqrt only after a nonnegative discriminant. This measured workload mix replaces the earlier all-root assumption; it is not a measured hardware speed.

With the same assumed 50 MHz, 1 GB/s aggregate payload bandwidth, batch size 1,024, 10 us launch/batch and 100 ns native packing/query, modeled core time is 80.1036 ms. Transfer is 18.6635 ms, launch 1.7600 ms and packing 17.9457 ms: 118.4728 ms total offload cost. Against the new full software time of 452.69625 ms, break-even requires removing more than 26.17% of release runtime.

T_new = T_full x (1 - f) + T_offload. f remains unknown: cProfile sphere share cannot supply it. The modeled 7% runtime reduction would require f > 33.17%; this is a sensitivity point, not a separate mandated hardware target. Batching can change early-exit queries and h, so the original query mix must be rechecked after integration.

The old all-root case against shadow-only software remains historical evidence, not the current default estimate. If applied to faster full software, that all-root stress case needs 71.90% removable time just to break even. No hardware improvement occurred between estimates; only software baseline and workload assumptions changed.

pages.title: A successful exact optimization, with bounded claims

blocks.text: The new complete session confirms flat_pow at 36.89% lower runtime, following the previous 37.53% result with identical source. It retains the power expression and exact accumulated state. Grouped showed that some local reuse was insufficient; full-state locality and explicit pair/position updates remove much more repeated work, reproduced in both native profiles and independent counter batches.

A five-body hardware engine could hold state locally and execute complete advance batches, amortizing transfer across 20,000 steps. It is not the implemented accelerator: exact agreement with the host nonintegral pow routine, dependencies between velocity updates and full trajectory validation make it a different, larger design. A MAC/rsqrt replacement would change rounding and is unsuitable for the strict final contract without further proof and testing.

One concrete ray-sphere HDL design satisfies the chosen single-component hardware scope. Its architecture and losing as well as winning estimate scenarios are documented above. It does not speed up nbody, and syntax checks are not a claim of numerical correctness or achieved acceleration.
